Old english text generator

This is the heavy, dramatic, 𝔬𝔩𝔡-𝔪𝔞𝔫𝔲𝔰𝔠𝔯𝔦𝔭𝔱 look — what people variously call Old English, gothic, blackletter, or by its proper name, fraktur. It maps your letters onto the Unicode fraktur set, in a regular weight and a bolder one for when the thin version gets lost on a busy background. It's a popular choice for tattoo mockups, band-ish logos, sports-team-style names, and bios that want to feel old and weighty. Real talk on the limits: fraktur is letters only — no numbers, no special punctuation — so digits stay plain, and a couple of the uppercase fraktur letters (the C and the I especially) look unusual enough that some people mistake them for other letters, which is just how that historic alphabet was drawn. It pastes into the usual places, though, like most decorative styles, the pickiest username fields will turn it down.

How to use it

Type in the box on the left. The style you’ve picked on the right updates as you type — no “generate” button. Click Copy and paste it wherever you need. On the home page you can also browse every style in the list below and click any row to load it into the panel.

Where it renders, and where it breaks

Fraktur is moderately well-supported — bios, captions and messages handle it fine. The quirks are the missing digits and a couple of capital letters that look like other letters.

All of these are real Unicode characters, not images or font files, so the styling travels with the text wherever you paste it. The catch: a few apps with locked-down fonts will draw some glyphs as empty boxes — that's the receiving app, not the text, and switching styles fixes it. Bold (sans), Small Caps and Full-width render the widest. Checked May 2026; platforms change their font handling constantly, so treat the table below as a strong guide, not a guarantee. Examples & use cases

The old, weighty look — where it fits:

  • Tattoo design mockup — Run a name or phrase through fraktur to show your artist the vibe — 𝔉𝔞𝔪𝔦𝔩𝔶, 𝔖𝔱𝔯𝔢𝔫𝔤𝔱𝔥. For the actual stencil, they'll use a real blackletter font; this is the reference.
  • Band-ish or team-ish name — Fraktur reads heavy and old, which is exactly the energy for a metal-band aesthetic or a sports-team-style handle. Bold fraktur if the thin one looks faint.
  • A dramatic bio line — 𝔠𝔥𝔞𝔬𝔰 𝔯𝔢𝔦𝔤𝔫𝔰 or similar — fraktur gives a bio gravitas (or melodrama, depending on taste). One line, not the whole bio.
  • Discord server / channel name — Discord renders fraktur cleanly in names, so a dramatic server name actually sticks here, unlike on Instagram where the username field fights you.
  • Bold fraktur for visibility — Against a photo or a colored banner, thin fraktur can disappear. Switch to 𝖇𝖔𝖑𝖉 𝖋𝖗𝖆𝖐𝖙𝖚𝖗 in the dropdown — same flavor, more weight.

Common mistakes

  • Don't put numbers in fraktur. There's no fraktur version of 0–9 in Unicode, so digits stay plain and the effect looks unfinished. Keep numbers out, or accept they'll be plain.
  • Don't be alarmed if a capital looks like the wrong letter. Historic blackletter drew certain capitals — notably C and I — in shapes that look strange to modern eyes. That's faithful to the original alphabet, not a glitch. If a reader might get confused, bold fraktur is a bit clearer.
  • Don't use this for an actual tattoo or print job. These are Unicode display characters, not a real typeface — they won't scale or print like a font file. As a mockup to show the look, fine. For the real thing, get a licensed blackletter font.
  • Don't expect it in a username. Fraktur usually gets rejected in username fields. For a name, bold sans is the fallback that passes most filters.

FAQ

Old English, gothic, blackletter, fraktur — are these all the same?
For copy-paste purposes, yes — they all point to the Unicode fraktur characters. "Old English font" is the search term most people use; "blackletter" and "fraktur" are the typographically correct names. Same letters either way.
Why don't numbers work in Old English text?
The Unicode fraktur range covers A–Z and a–z only. There's no fraktur set for 0–9 or most punctuation, so this tool leaves them as normal characters rather than substituting something that doesn't match.
Can I use this for a tattoo design?
As a mockup or to show your artist the vibe, sure. For the actual stencil you (or they) should use a proper blackletter font file — these Unicode characters aren't a real typeface and won't scale or print the way a font will.
Some capital letters look like the wrong letter — why?
Historic blackletter drew certain capitals — notably C, I, and a few others — in shapes that look strange to modern eyes. That's faithful to the original alphabet, not a glitch. If a reader might get confused, the bold fraktur version is a bit clearer.
Fraktur vs. bold fraktur — when do I switch?
Use bold fraktur (𝖋𝖗𝖆𝖐𝖙𝖚𝖗) when the thin version (𝔣𝔯𝔞𝔨𝔱𝔲𝔯) gets lost — against a photo, a colored banner, at small sizes. It's the same letterforms with more weight, so it stays legible where the regular one fades.
Will Old English text show up on everyone's phone?
Mostly. A few older Androids and stock keyboards don't include the fraktur glyphs and show boxes — that's their font, not your text. Bold fraktur renders in some places the thin one doesn't; bold sans is the universal fallback.
